# V&V Re-Check: SFCC-237 Undici Connection Pool Isolation Claim

I independently re-verified all 11 items against the current state of the repo (branch `develop`, clean except unrelated translation-compile diffs). **Bottom line up front: the original claim holds up on every point I could test. I found no evidence contradicting "7 pools defined, 0 wired up, 0 in-process failure isolation today."** I did find several genuinely new, non-contradicting pieces of context (governance reason for the gap, and which of the 7 pools even have live code behind them yet) that sharpen the finding — flagged clearly below.

---

## 1. `overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts` — full read

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding**, with one precision note.

The file (`/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/overrides/app/ssr/connectionPools.ts`, 76 lines) defines exactly 7 `Pool` instances from `undici` (line 19: `import { Pool } from 'undici';`):

| Export (code, line) | Origin | connections | connectTimeout | bodyTimeout |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sfccScapiPool` (L22-25) | `` `https://${COMMERCE_API_SHORT_CODE}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com}` `` | 5 | 5_000 | 8_000 |
| `sfccPaymentsPool` (L33-36) | `SFCC_PAYMENTS_HOST` env, placeholder fallback | 10 | 5_000 | 8_000 |
| `mulesoftPool` (L42-46) | `MULESOFT_BASE_URL` env, placeholder fallback | 20 | 5_000 | 10_000 |
| `marketingCloudAuthPool` (L49-52) | `` `https://${MARKETING_CLOUD_SUBDOMAIN}.auth.marketingcloudapis.com}` `` | 5 | 5_000 | 15_000 |
| `marketingCloudRestPool` (L55-58) | `` `https://${MARKETING_CLOUD_SUBDOMAIN}.rest.marketingcloudapis.com}` `` | 5 | 5_000 | 15_000 |
| `googlePlacesPool` (L61-65) | `'https://places.googleapis.com'` | 5 | 3_000 | 5_000 |
| `booxiPool` (L71-75) | `BOOXI_BASE_URL` env, placeholder fallback | 5 | 3_000 | 5_000 |

This is a 1:1 numeric match with the "7 pools with the same names/caps" description, and with the docs (items 8/9 below). **Precision note:** the *literal string names* `sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, etc. do not appear as string values anywhere in this file (`Pool()` takes a positional origin URL, not a name) — those kebab-case identifiers are the docs' table labels, not code tokens. The code's actual export identifiers are `sfccScapiPool`, `sfccPaymentsPool`, `mulesoftPool`, `marketingCloudAuthPool`, `marketingCloudRestPool`, `googlePlacesPool`, `booxiPool`. Conceptually these are unambiguously the same 7 pools — this is a naming-convention difference, not a discrepancy in substance.

Also note the file's own doc-comment (L1-18) explicitly frames this as **not yet wired up**: *"Use the per-call `dispatcher` option on `fetch()` calls inside ssr.js to route requests through the correct pool"* (L5-6) — phrased as an instruction for future work, not a description of existing behavior. Two of the seven (`sfccPaymentsPool`, `booxiPool`) carry explicit `TODO`s (L30-31, L69) saying their real origin hostnames are still unconfirmed placeholders.

## 2. Repo-wide grep for every plausible reference

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding.** Every single hit outside `connectionPools.ts` is either documentation/rules prose or unrelated noise. None wire a pool into a real fetch call.

- **`connectionPools`** (4 hits total): the file's own self-reference in its doc-comment (`connectionPools.ts:9`), plus 3 governance/rules docs describing it as a protected file (`.cursor/rules/tier1FrozenFiles.mdc:55`, `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md:48`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md:381`) — all read `connectionPools.ts — undici pool isolation (blast-radius mitigation)` in a file-ownership table, not code.
- **`dispatcher`** (case-insensitive, 6 hits): `connectionPools.ts:5,10` (the file's own doc-comment example), `.docs/architecture.md:261,275`, `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md:471,473` (documentation prose), and one false positive — `package-lock.json:36539: "storybook": "dist/bin/dispatcher.js"` — Storybook's own CLI binary path, unrelated to undici.
- **`undici`** (case-insensitive, ~13 hits): `connectionPools.ts:2,8,13,19` (the real usage), `package-lock.json` transitive dependency entries (`undici-types` pulled in by `@formatjs/ts-transformer`; `undici` itself pulled in as `^7.25.0` under some other package's nested `node_modules` — **not a direct dependency of this app**, see item 6), and doc prose in `.docs/architecture.md` / `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` / `.docs/temp/openItems.md:48` / `.docs/integration/01-sfcc.md:141`.
- **Each of the 7 pool export names individually**: every one of `sfccScapiPool`, `sfccPaymentsPool`, `mulesoftPool`, `marketingCloudAuthPool`, `marketingCloudRestPool`, `googlePlacesPool`, `booxiPool` appears **only inside `connectionPools.ts` itself** (its own `export const` line, plus one internal cross-reference comment for `sfccScapiPool` at L29, and the doc-comment's illustrative import at L9 for `sfccPaymentsPool`). **Zero hits in `ssr.js` or any of the four handler files.** No file anywhere imports any of these seven names.
- **`Pool(`** (the undici constructor call): the 7 real calls in `connectionPools.ts` (L22, 33, 42, 49, 55, 61, 71), plus one more hit — `.docs/architecture.md:267: const checkoutPool = new Pool('https://api.checkout-service.com', {` — this is a **fictional, illustrative tutorial snippet** embedded in the doc (fake pool name, fake origin, not a real file or import path in the repo). It's worth flagging precisely because it's literally a worked example of what wiring *would* look like — and the real code doesn't do it.
- **`setGlobalDispatcher`**: exactly 1 hit, in prose only — `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md:473`, a comparative note ("the per-call `dispatcher` option is safer than the `setGlobalDispatcher`..."). **Zero calls to `setGlobalDispatcher` anywhere in actual code.**

## 3. Full content of every `overrides/app/ssr/` file + `ssr.js` — every `fetch()` call

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding.** I read all 6 files in `overrides/app/ssr/` (confirmed exactly these 6 exist, no new file added: `connectionPools.ts`, `contentSecurityPolicy.ts`, `marketingCloud.ts`, `paymentMetadata.ts`, `slasTokens.ts`, `types.ts`) plus `overrides/app/ssr.js`. `contentSecurityPolicy.ts` (CSP directives object) and `types.ts` (TS interfaces) contain **zero** `fetch()` calls. `ssr.js` itself contains **zero** direct `fetch()` calls — it only wires Express routes and delegates to the handler functions imported from `./ssr/*`.

I found exactly **4 fetch calls** total, and quote each in full — **none has a `dispatcher` key**:

1. **`overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts:78`**
   ```js
   const response = await fetch(JWKS_URI);
   ```
   No options object at all — `dispatcher` **absent** (trivially).

2. **`overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts:42-44`**
   ```js
   const response = await fetch(app.sfPayments.metadataUrl, {
     headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
   });
   ```
   `dispatcher` **absent**.

3. **`overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts:38-46`**
   ```js
   const tokenResponse = await fetch(tokenUrl, {
     method: 'POST',
     headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
     body: JSON.stringify({
       grant_type: 'client_credentials',
       client_id: clientId,
       client_secret: clientSecret,
     }),
   });
   ```
   `dispatcher` **absent**.

4. **`overrides/app/ssr/marketingCloud.ts:61-75`**
   ```js
   const emailResponse = await fetch(emailUrl, {
     method: 'POST',
     headers: {
       Authorization: `Bearer ${marketingCloudToken}`,
       'Content-Type': 'application/json',
     },
     body: JSON.stringify({
       definitionKey: marketingCloudConfig.templateId,
       recipient: {
         contactKey: emailId,
         to: emailId,
         attributes: { 'magic-link': marketingCloudConfig.magicLink },
       },
     }),
   });
   ```
   `dispatcher` **absent**.

**4 of 4 live fetch calls in the SSR layer lack the dispatcher option** — direct, concrete confirmation of the claim for the code paths that actually run today.

## 4. `overrides/app/request-processor.js` and `worker/main.js`

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding.**

- **`overrides/app/request-processor.js`** (119 lines) is still the **unmodified PWA Kit example/boilerplate**. Its own header says: *"This is an EXAMPLE file. To enable request processing, rename it to 'request-processor.js' and update the `processRequest` function..."* (L8-9) and explicitly warns *"Do not make external requests from this code"* (L20-21). The body only strips query-string parameters (e.g. `usid`/`code` on `/callback`) and has bot-detection logic commented out (L104-112). It contains **zero** network calls, zero isolation/resilience logic. (Corroborated independently by `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md:60`: *"`overrides/app/request-processor.js` — add here when populated."* — i.e., the project's own governance doc confirms this file is still unpopulated.)
- **`worker/main.js`** is a **7-line stub** — nothing but the BSD-3-Clause license header comment. Zero code, zero logic of any kind.

Neither file contains any isolation/resilience mechanism.

## 5. `git log` for the 7 SSR-related files

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding.** Verified via `git log --oneline --follow` on `develop`, and cross-checked with `git log --all` (every local + remote branch) — identical results, no other branch has additional commits:

| File | Commits (hash / date / subject) |
|---|---|
| `connectionPools.ts` | **`610020e` / 2026-06-19 / "refactor(ssr): split ssr.js into typed helper modules"** — only commit ever |
| `slasTokens.ts` | `2484515` / 2026-06-26 / "chore: ESLint fixes"; `610020e` / 2026-06-19 / same as above |
| `paymentMetadata.ts` | `610020e` / 2026-06-19 / same — only commit |
| `marketingCloud.ts` | `2484515` / 2026-06-26 / "chore: ESLint fixes"; `610020e` / 2026-06-19 / same |
| `ssr.js` | `610020e` / 2026-06-19 / same; `3cfc0d9` / 2026-06-12 / "fix(config): hardcode dev1 proxy hosts, enable SLAS private client, add dev1 env config"; `cd60b7a` / 2026-06-12 / "Initial commit during Detailed Design phase" |
| `request-processor.js` | `cd60b7a` / 2026-06-12 / "Initial commit during Detailed Design phase" — only commit |
| `worker/main.js` | `cd60b7a` / 2026-06-12 / same — only commit |

`connectionPools.ts` has **never been touched since the day it was created** (2026-06-19). Nothing in this set has changed in **~7 weeks** relative to today (2026-08-11). This directly confirms nothing has changed since the claim was last checked.

## 6. `package.json` dependencies/devDependencies — resilience libraries

**CONFIRMED — none exist.** Full contents read at `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/package.json`:

- `"dependencies"` (L114-118): `@contentful/experiences-sdk-react`, `@contentful/live-preview`, `contentful` — only 3 entries, all Contentful-related.
- `"devDependencies"` (L21-41): `@playwright/test`, `@salesforce/retail-react-app`, Storybook packages, `husky`, `jsdom`, `semver`, `ts-morph`, `typescript`, `vitest`, etc. — 18 entries.

No `opossum`, `cockatiel`, `p-retry`, `p-timeout`, or `undici` anywhere in either list. `undici` and `p-timeout` appear **only** in `package-lock.json` as transitive dependencies of other packages (not requested by this app's own `package.json`), so they are not an "other isolation mechanism" available to app code.

## 7. Test files referencing `connectionPools`, `dispatcher`, or the 4 SSR handlers

None of them — nor any other file in the repo — reference `connectionPools`, `dispatcher`, `slasTokens`, `paymentMetadata`, `marketingCloud`, `jwksCaching`, `validateSlasCallbackToken`, `paymentMetadataHandler`, or `sendMagicLinkEmail`, except the source files themselves and the three governance/rules docs already cited in item 2. There is **zero test coverage** of the pools or the four SSR handler files. (Side note, not from repo content but from this session's own task tracker: there is a pending item "*Implement Vitest blast-radius proof suite (tests 1-3)*" — i.e. this gap is already recognized as unaddressed work, not something I'm asserting new.)

## 8. `.docs/architecture.md` — "Blast-Radius Mitigation" section, verbatim

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding, essentially verbatim.** Full section is lines 257-291:

> **## Blast-Radius Mitigation** (L257)
>
> Multiple upstream integrations (SFCC, MuleSoft/Omneo, Global-e, Narvar, Contentful, Didomi, Inside Chat) mean a failure or attack targeting one service must not cascade. A PWA-relevant mitigation can be done in the SSR layer. (L259)
>
> The SSR layer in `overrides/app/ssr.js` uses **Node's native `fetch`**, which is backed by `undici`. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS). (L261)

This matches the remembered quote's two fragments exactly (word-for-word). Lines 263-278 contain the same illustrative `checkoutPool` code example noted in item 2. Lines 282-290 contain the 7-pool table (`sfcc-scapi`/5, `sfcc-payments`/10, `mulesoft`/20, `marketing-cloud-auth`/5, `marketing-cloud-rest`/5, `google-places`/5, `booxi`/5), numerically identical to `connectionPools.ts` and to item 9's table below. Line 280 explicitly labels these "**Planned** pools" — present tense, still not built as of today.

**Via `git blame`**, this exact section was authored by commit `c8157619` (2026-06-17) and last touched by `4be80965` (2026-07-10, table-formatting only). The file's most recent commit overall, `7d9c4af` (2026-07-16), did **not** touch this section (confirmed by blame — no lines in 257-291 attributed to it).

## 9. `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md` §12 and §12.1, verbatim

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding**, plus important supporting nuance not previously called out.

**§12 "Graceful Degradation"** (L445-458) — opens: *"Each external system fails independently — one outage does not break a page."* (L447), followed by a per-system failure-mode table (Contentful, Global-e, Didomi, Omneo writes/reads, Google Maps, AP21, Narvar).

**§12.1 "Blast-Radius Containment"** (L460-487), full verbatim text:

> ### 12.1 Blast-Radius Containment (L460)
>
> The failure modes above describe what the PWA does when a single integration is unavailable. This section covers how to limit the *spread* of an attack or outage — ensuring a degraded integration cannot consume shared resources and take down unrelated features. (L462)
>
> #### Edge (outside the PWA — Infrastructure / SI Partner) (L464)
> - **Web Application Firewalls + rate limiting** is the primary lever for volumetric attacks and credential-stuffing.
> - **SFCC Business Manager** provides API-level rate limiting for SFCC endpoints, independent of the storefront edge. (L466-467)
>
> #### SSR layer (inside the PWA) (L469)
>
> `overrides/app/ssr.js` makes server-side `fetch` calls directly (token exchange, JWKS, SF Payments metadata). Node's native `fetch` is backed by `undici` internally. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS). (L471)
>
> > **Implementation note:** the per-call `dispatcher` option is safer than the `setGlobalDispatcher` in a managed environment (MRT) since it does not touch the global dispatcher that Salesforce internal libraries may rely on. The `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client server-side (Commerce SDK) and are not affected in either approach. (L473)
>
> [same 7-pool table as architecture.md, L477-485, identical names/caps/timeouts]
>
> **Contentful:** The Contentful SDK (`contentful` v11) does not expose a `dispatcher` hook on its internal fetch calls, so connection isolation for Contentful is not achievable through this pattern. Primary mitigation is the graceful degradation rule in §12 (Render page without editorial content). (L487)

This matches the remembered "7 pools with the same names/caps" exactly. **Two trivial wording diffs vs. architecture.md's copy of the table** (not a substantive disagreement): the `sfcc-payments` row says *"waiting confirmation from Mani"* here (L480) vs. *"confirm with Integration team"* in architecture.md; the `booxi` row says *"TBD"* (L485) here vs. *"TBD — confirm with Integration team"* in architecture.md.

**Genuinely new context worth surfacing (does not contradict the claim, but sharpens it):**
- §12.1 itself draws the exact scoping the original claim uses — it explicitly separates "Edge (outside the PWA)" mitigations (WAF, rate limiting, SFCC Business Manager) from "SSR layer (inside the PWA)" mitigations. So there *is* some blast-radius protection in the overall system — just not inside the Node process, which is precisely what the claim is scoped to. This is corroboration, not contradiction.
- L473 states plainly that `commerce-sdk-react` hooks (i.e., most real SFCC commerce traffic — PDP/PLP/cart/basket) "manage their own HTTP client... and are not affected in either approach" — meaning the 7-pool mechanism was **never designed** to cover the bulk of SFCC traffic, only the four direct-`fetch()` SSR endpoints.
- L487 confirms Contentful — likely the highest-volume SSR-side call — is explicitly **out of scope** for this mechanism by design (SDK limitation), with graceful degradation as the only mitigation.

## 10. `git log` for both docs files

**CONFIRMED — matches prior finding**, both have commit history, but the actual blast-radius content is stale relative to "today."

- **`.docs/architecture.md`**: 11 commits from `cd60b7a` (2026-06-12) through `7d9c4af` (2026-07-16). Full list: `7d9c4af`(07-16) `578d10e`(07-13) `4be8096`(07-10) `42bb484`(07-02) `d42dbd2`(06-24) `2c9e49f`(06-24) `8c2e6b4`(06-23) `4b8a18d`(06-20) `c815761`(06-17) `d9ad453`(06-15) `cd60b7a`(06-12).
- **`.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md`**: 15 commits from `cd60b7a`(06-12) through `2224db3`(07-16). Full list: `2224db3`(07-16) `7d9c4af`(07-16) `19c23fb`(07-16) `2339714`(07-16) `f5af7be`(07-16) `578d10e`(07-13) `4be8096`(07-10) `8eb1e2d`(07-08) `d5012bc`(07-03) `c3bb2fd`(06-27) `de397b9`(06-26) `42bb484`(07-02) `d42dbd2`(06-24) `2c9e49f`(06-24) `4b8a18d`(06-20) `c815761`(06-17) `d9ad453`(06-15) `cd60b7a`(06-12).

I went further and verified via `git blame` + `git show --stat` on the most recent commit to each file that **the Blast-Radius content specifically was not touched recently**: the last commit to `tsd-architecture.md`, `2224db3` (2026-07-16, "fix: resolve CodeRabbit findings from PR #37 review"), only edited a Stage/UAT topology table plus 4 other unrelated docs (`projectState.md`, `releaseBranchesRules.md`, `openItems.md`, `README.md`) — confirmed by its diffstat (`.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md | 4 ++--`), nowhere near §12/§12.1. ## 11. Broader unbiased sweep for other resilience mechanisms

This is where I actively hunted for something that would contradict the claim. **I found nothing that contradicts it**, but I found three adjacent, genuinely new items worth flagging transparently — none of them provide in-process isolation for the shared Node/MRT SSR runtime:

- **`circuit breaker`**: 0 hits anywhere in the repo.
- **`bulkhead`**: 0 hits anywhere in the repo.
- **`AbortController`**: 2 hits, both in **`overrides/app/hooks/useContentful.ts`** (L31, L94) inside `useContentfulEntry`/`useContentfulEntries`. **NEW FINDING, but does not contradict the claim** — this is client-side React (browser) code (`useState`/`useEffect` hooks fetching directly from `cdn.contentful.com`/`preview.contentful.com`), not server-side SSR code, and it's a standard React "cancel in-flight request on unmount/dependency change" pattern (`return () => controller.abort()`), not a timeout or circuit-breaker — no `setTimeout` is ever wired to the controller. It runs in a different process (the browser) from the shared Node MRT process the claim is about.
- **`AbortSignal.timeout`**: 4 hits, in **`scripts/switchEnv.mjs`** (L690, L733) and **`scripts/sfcc/_shared.mjs`** (L81, L108). **NEW FINDING, but does not contradict the claim** — these are genuine request timeouts, but they live in standalone developer-run CLI tooling (`npm run env`, SFCC site-config sync scripts), executed manually outside the deployed storefront's request-handling process. They don't run in, and have no effect on, the production Node/MRT process serving shopper traffic.
- **`p-timeout`**: 0 direct hits; appears only inside `package-lock.json` as some other package's transitive dependency — not used by any app code.
- **`retry`** (broad sweep, ~50 hits): the overwhelming majority are non-code — UI copy/translation strings (`"account.payments.action.retry": "Retry"`), Playwright CI test-retry config (`playwright.config.js:29,48` — test-runner retries, unrelated to production resilience), and documentation describing **third parties'** own retry behavior (MuleSoft's "Failover-Reversal 2.0", Global-e's own retry mechanism, Adyen Drop-in's own retry, Contentful 429 "exponential backoff and retry" as a documented expectation with no corresponding code found). The one substantive **app-code** hit is **`overrides/app/components/_app-config/index.tsx:222-236`**, which explicitly sets TanStack Query's `retry: false` (queries and mutations) and `retryOnMount: false` (server-side only) — i.e., **retries are deliberately disabled**, the opposite of a resilience mechanism. This doesn't provide isolation either; it just means a failed call fails once and stops, per the comment "Recommended settings for PWA-Kit usages" (L219).

**Additional finding beyond the literal 11-item checklist, surfaced because it materially sharpens the picture:** I checked whether the integrations behind 3 of the 7 pools (`mulesoft`, `google-places`, `booxi`) have *any* implemented call path elsewhere in the repo (components, `config/*.js` `proxyConfigs`, env files) that might bypass `ssr.js` entirely. They do not:
- `config/default.js:209-218`'s `proxyConfigs` array contains only two SFCC entries (`api`, `ocapi`) — no MuleSoft/Google/Booxi proxy config exists.
- `.env.sample:179` shows `MULESOFT_BASE_URL=` blank/unset.
- `.docs/prd/account.md:230,297` and `.docs/integration/06-booxi.md`/`index.md:27` describe Booxi appointment history as still **"scope/timeline TBC"** — not yet built.
- No `places.googleapis.com` fetch exists outside `connectionPools.ts` itself and the CSP allow-list (`contentSecurityPolicy.ts:23,53`, which merely permits the domain, it doesn't call it).

This means **4 of the 7 pools** (`sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, `marketing-cloud-auth`, `marketing-cloud-rest`) correspond to integrations with real, currently-shipping `fetch()` calls that concretely bypass their pool today (proven in item 3), while the other **3** (`mulesoft`, `google-places`, `booxi`) correspond to features that have **no implementation at all** in this repo yet — those pools were built speculatively, ahead of the feature code that would eventually need them. Both groups are still accurately described as "100% unused" — this just clarifies *why*, and that the "isolation" story for 3 of the 7 hasn't even reached the stage of having something to isolate.

**Also worth surfacing (governance context, explains *why* nothing has changed, doesn't change the technical fact):** `connectionPools.ts` and the whole `overrides/app/ssr/` directory are listed as **Tier 1 "Frozen Files"** in three separate project rule docs — `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md:42-58`, `.cursor/rules/tier1FrozenFiles.mdc`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md:381` — owned by "Integration / SI Partner," with the rule: *"These files must not be modified by Claude Code without the developer explicitly naming the file in the prompt AND confirming they have spoken to the listed owner. No exceptions."* This is a plausible institutional reason the gap has persisted (a deliberate change-control gate, not simple oversight) — but it doesn't alter the current-state fact: today, the pools are unused and there is no in-process failure isolation.

---

### Overall verdict

Across all 11 items, **I found nothing that contradicts or changes the original claim**. The claim — 7 undici pools defined in `connectionPools.ts`, zero wiring anywhere else in the codebase (zero imports, zero `dispatcher` usage, zero `Pool(` calls outside the one file, zero test coverage), all 4 live SSR fetch calls confirmed dispatcher-less, no alternative circuit-breaker/bulkhead/resilience library in `package.json`, and no code change to any of the 7 relevant files in ~7 weeks — is **fully substantiated** by direct, current-state inspection. The only things this pass adds are clarifying, non-contradicting context: the governance reason the file is frozen, the split between "pools bypassed by live code" (4) vs. "pools built ahead of unimplemented features" (3), and a few unrelated timeout/cancellation patterns elsewhere (browser-side Contentful hook, dev-tooling scripts) that don't provide in-process isolation for the shared Node/MRT server and thus don't change the "zero failure isolation in the single shared Node process" conclusion.

*Last updated 2026-07-16. Scope: architecture — stack, customisation model, integrations, regional/multi-site, SSR/SEO, performance, accessibility, testing, CI/CD. Requirement IDs (e.g. DMU-030, REG-041) reference the **Zimmermann Functional Requirements** spreadsheet.*

---

1. Purpose & Scope
------------------

This TSD describes the technical foundation for the Zimmermann production storefront at <http://www.zimmermann.com> — a luxury Australian fashion brand running on Salesforce Commerce Cloud (SFCC) PWA Kit.

**In scope:**

* Stack and build pipeline
* The customisation model on top of `@salesforce/retail-react-app`
* Multi-site / multi-locale routing across 8 storefronts in 6 regions
* Integration map (SFCC, MuleSoft, Contentful, Global-e, Didomi, Adyen, Omneo, Narvar, GiveX, Google Places)
* SSR + SEO foundation (DMU-030, hreflang, sitemaps, structured data)
* Performance budgets, accessibility, consent gating, GDPR
* Testing strategy and CI/CD topology
* Open decisions requiring client input before build

**Out of scope:** per-feature functional design; detailed per-vendor integration design

---

2. Solution Overview
--------------------

A single PWA Kit codebase serves 8 logical SFCC sites, each with its own currency, tax model, locale set, delivery options, payment methods, and consent defaults. International checkout is owned by Global-e; domestic checkout is owned by SFCC. All order-creation, fulfilment write, and CRM sync traffic from SFCC routes through **MuleSoft** as the middleware boundary — SFCC does not call NewStore, AP21, Omneo, or Narvar directly. In addition, the PWA's MRT Node layer calls MuleSoft directly (via `/mobify/proxy/mulesoft/...`) for read operations: order history, order details, boutique stock checks (Find in Boutique, Collect in Boutique), GiveX balance check, and real-time stock availability. These reads bypass SFCC entirely.

The PWA itself also talks to a handful of services without going through SFCC. Contentful and Didomi are browser-direct. Google Maps (Places API), GiveX balance check (proxied through MuleSoft — see §2 GiveX note), and select MuleSoft operations are called from the PWA's MRT Node layer via proxy, with API credentials held server-side as MRT environment variables.

4. Customisation Model
----------------------

This project uses the Salesforce PWA Kit's *template extensibility* model. `@salesforce/retail-react-app` is consumed as an unmodified npm dependency, not a forked copy of the repository.

All customisations live in an `overrides/` directory that mirrors the structure of the underlying `@salesforce/retail-react-app` package. The base package is consumed unmodified — overrides take precedence at resolution time. This keeps the project upgradeable: pulling a new Salesforce baseline is a dependency bump plus a targeted reconciliation of overridden files, not a full re-application of patches.

**Working principle:** stay as close to base PWA Kit behaviour as possible. Visual changes (Chakra props, theme tokens, SCSS where Chakra is insufficient) are expected. Structural changes (data flow, routing, or layout deviations from the base template) are taken deliberately and reviewed against the upgrade impact before being merged.

**Brand-new components** (with no base equivalent) will also live in the `overrides/` folder.

### 4.1 Environment Configuration

All secrets and per-tier identifiers are injected as **Managed Runtime environment variables**. Unless public identifiers, they must never be committed to source control or exposed in client-side bundles. The canonical list of every variable the storefront expects is maintained in the project's environment-variable template, grouped by integration with inline comments — that template is the single source of truth. **Security policy:**

* Real values live only in local, untracked environment files — one shared file (`.env.shared`, tier-independent) plus one per deployment tier (`.env.<tier>` for dev/test/sit/uat/staging/prod), managed via `npm run env` (`scripts/switchEnv.mjs`). Only a template — variable names tagged `# scope:shared|tier|personal|auto` on their own comment line, no secret values — is committed to source control as `.env.sample`. Two guardrails enforce this: a pre-commit hook that blocks commit if `.env.sample` contains a secret-shaped non-empty value, and a Claude Code rule that instructs the AI assistant never to write real secret values into `.env.sample`.
* Public identifiers (e.g. the GTM container ID, Didomi notice ID, SFCC SLAS client ID) may carry placeholder values in the committed template.
* Secrets (tokens, license keys, HMAC secrets, server-side API keys) appear in the committed template as the variable name only, with an empty value.
* Non-personal shared/tier values can be centrally published and pulled via this repo's GitHub Environments (`shared` + one per deployment tier under Settings > Environments), stored as GitHub Environment Variables — write access requires repo Admin (`@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers`), read access is repo-collaborator-wide. This is a deliberate, documented exception to using GitHub Secrets (which cannot be read back via API once set) — see `.env.sample`'s header for the full rationale. Genuinely personal credentials (`scope:personal` — your own Jira/Confluence token, your own Contentful CMA token) are always excluded from this and never centralized.
* MRT variables are managed per environment (Dev / SIT / Stage / UAT / Prod) in the Managed Runtime console and rotated independently of the codebase.

5. Multi-Site, Multi-Locale Architecture
----------------------------------------

### 5.1 Storefronts

**8 independent SFCC sites across 6 regions**, each with its own currency, tax model, locale set, delivery options, and payment methods. 11 active locales total. US/EU domestic and international are configured as separate SFCC sites (REG-006).

| Locale | URL prefix | Currency | Checkout owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AU + Oceania | `/` (x-default hreflang) | AUD | SFCC (REG-003) |
| UK | `/uk/` | GBP | SFCC (REG-004) |
| US domestic | `/us/` | USD | SFCC (REG-005) |
| US international | `/en-ca/` | USD | Global-e (REG-005) |
| EU domestic — EN / FR / IT / ES | `/en-eu/`, `/fr-eu/`, `/it-eu/`, `/es-eu/` | EUR | SFCC (REG-006 dom) |
| EU international | `/en-ch/` | EUR | Global-e (REG-006 intl) |
| HK | `/hk/` | HKD (Global-e display) | Global-e (REG-007) |
| ME | `/en-ae/` | AED (Global-e display) | Global-e (REG-008) |

Rest-of-world traffic routes via `/en-ch/` and `/en-ca/` (DMU-013). AU is configured at the root with no locale prefix and serves as the x-default hreflang target (DMU-016).

### 5.2 Entry routing

* **IP geolocation** selects the site on first visit (REG-013).
* **AU is gated** to Oceania IPs only (REG-009) but remains the x-default hreflang target, so gating runs in the application layer rather than at the network. Non-Oceania human visitors are redirected server-side to their matched storefront before AUD pricing renders; verified search-engine and social-unfurler bots are exempt; UA ambiguity fails open (false positives have no SEO cost; missing a real crawler does).
* **Cross-region entry handling for all other storefronts** — first-visit mismatch-detection slide-out, the country/language selector, and the EU language-mismatch modal — is functional design (REG-014–035), out of scope for this TSD.

### 5.3 Single source of truth for country / locale

Country, locale, currency, shipping country, Global-e flag, and boutique-region data live in a single front-end configuration module. When a market is added, that module and the SFCC site configuration are updated together.

### 5.4 Per-storefront concerns that must not bleed

* **Consent defaults (REG-054):** per-storefront Didomi defaults are site-scoped config that must not bleed across storefronts; the values themselves are specified under REG-054.
* **Tax model:** SFCC native tax tables (AU GST, UK VAT); Avalara for US domestic, NZ, New Caledonia, and EU domestic (EU domestic added 2026-06-19); Global-e handles tax for international checkout paths.
* **Marketing opt-in default (REG-057):** site-scoped per storefront; must not bleed — value specified under REG-057.
* **Payment methods:** per-storefront Adyen configuration. Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Klarna are post-launch.

### 5.5 Session and basket scope across storefronts

All eight storefronts are path-prefixed on a single first-party domain and run on a single SFCC realm with shared customer data. This determines how a shopper's session behaves when they cross storefronts (via the country / language selector or the mismatch slide-out):

* **Session cookie is shared.** The `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie set by the SSR layer is first-party to the one domain, so it is presented on requests to any storefront prefix — no cross-domain SSO bridge is needed.
* **Tokens are channel-scoped.** A SLAS token carries the site it was issued for, so the SSR layer re-initialises the SLAS context for the destination storefront. Because the customer record is shared across the realm, a registered shopper is silently re-recognised without re-entering credentials; a guest session is site-scoped and does not carry over.
* **Basket does not transfer — by design.** Baskets are site-scoped and priced in the storefront's own currency against its own pricebook, so a shopper switching storefront starts a fresh basket. Carrying a basket across a currency / pricebook boundary would produce incorrect pricing.
* **Checkout handoff is separate.** When an international storefront hands off to Global-e, the SLAS session does not extend into the Global-e hosted checkout — Global-e owns that session in full.

6. Checkout Ownership Branching
-------------------------------

Checkout owner is determined at PDP / cart, not only at the checkout page — so price, shipping, duty, and tax presentation are correct before the customer commits.

* **SFCC owns:** AU domestic (including Oceania — Avalara for NZ + New Caledonia), UK, US (when shipping to US), EU domestic.
* **Global-e owns:** HK, ME, EU international, the US site when shipping outside the US, and any domestic storefront when the selected shipping destination is outside that storefront's market.
* **Pricing for Global-e markets (REG-041):** SFCC holds all pricebooks (including Global-e ones), derived nightly from AP21 base prices and Global-e FX/coefficients. SFCC sends the complete cart in target currency at handoff; Global-e owns shipping, duties, and tax from that point. Full mechanism specified under PRC-34..43.
* **Global-e shipping country lock (REG-028):** locked at the country selector pre-checkout; cannot change once inside Global-e.

7. Integration Map
------------------

### 7.1 Classification model

Every integration is placed in one of five **boundary classes** based on where its network call originates. The split is determined by the vendor's documented auth model — a publishable key implies browser-direct is safe; a secret key forces a server-side hop.

* **Browser-direct** — call originates from the user's browser. Vendor publishes a publishable/public key designed to ship in the JS bundle (with referrer or origin restrictions where applicable). No secret material is ever exposed.
* **MRT-mediated** — call originates from the Node layer that hosts PWA Kit (the SSR pass, a server-only proxy endpoint in the SSR/Node layer, the `/mobify/proxy/` forwarding layer, or a webhook receiver). Used whenever the vendor requires a secret token, whenever an API key must be kept off the browser bundle entirely, or whenever `httpOnly` cookies must be set or read. Credentials are held as MRT environment variables. This includes calls the PWA makes directly to MuleSoft via MRT proxy (rather than routing through SFCC).
* **SFCC-cartridge** — call originates from inside Salesforce Commerce Cloud (a Demandware cartridge). The PWA never makes the call; credentials live in SFCC Business Manager.
* **via MuleSoft** — SFCC-side, server-to-server through the MuleSoft middleware. The PWA never sees the downstream system.
* **Out-of-band** — runs outside the storefront runtime entirely (scheduled feed, build-time pipeline, or system-to-system integration that bypasses the PWA and often SFCC too).

A single integration can span multiple classes — e.g. Adyen is `SFCC-cartridge` for `/payments` calls and `Browser-direct` for the Drop-In SDK; Global-e is `Browser-direct` (checkout handoff — iframe embed) and `SFCC-cartridge` (pricing feed); GiveX is `via MuleSoft` / server-side NewStore-adapter for issue/validate/redeem/refund and `MRT-mediated` for balance checks. Compound rows list every class that applies.

> Reading the table: **Call origin** = where the network request is issued from. **Hosting layer** = which boundary class above. **Security** = how credentials are exposed.

---

8. SSR, SEO, and GEO Foundation
-------------------------------

### 8.1 SSR (DMU-030)

All product, category, and content pages will use SSR for full crawlability by search engines and AI bots without dependence on client-side JS. The PWA Kit SSR pipeline is preserved end-to-end. Componentry that cannot SSR is rendered through a hydration-safe boundary that still emits SEO-relevant markup on the server. Global state stores are initialised per request to prevent state leaking across SSR responses.

#### 8.1.1 SSR vs CSR by page type

PWA Kit always runs the SSR pipeline — every page is server-rendered to some degree. The practical distinction is what content is rendered on the server vs fetched after hydration on the client.

| Page type | Pattern | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PDP, PLP, content pages, homepages, boutique pages | **Full SSR** — markup and data rendered on the server | Indexable, SEO- and LCP-critical |
| Cart, checkout, My Account, order history, wishlist, address book | **SSR shell + CSR data** — server renders the layout, header, footer, and skeleton; `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` hydrates personalised data (basket lines, customer profile, orders) client-side after hydration | Personalised, per-session, behind authentication. No SEO value (blocked in `robots.txt` — §8.3). Server-rendering personalised data would defeat edge caching and risk state leaking across requests |
| Search results, filtered PLP states | **SSR shell + CSR data** | Blocked in `robots.txt`; filter / sort state is client-driven |

The "SSR shell + CSR data" pattern still gives the user instant first paint of the page chrome — only the personalised payload waits on hydration. No page is purely client-rendered.

### 8.2 Canonicals & hreflang

Canonical tags on every indexable page; filtered PLPs canonicalise to the unfiltered base PLP. hreflang on canonical PDPs only, delivered via XML sitemap, consolidated to ~12 regional/language-level tags. Detailed canonical/hreflang rules are specified in the functional requirements.

### 8.3 Sitemaps & robots

Per-storefront / per-locale XML sitemaps refreshed daily, excluding disabled and deleted pages (DMU-026). `robots.txt` permits indexable pages (including the bag page) and blocks checkout, account, search results, and filtered URL parameters. URLs blocked in `robots.txt` never appear in a sitemap.

### 8.4 Structured data

Custom JSON-LD per the Sparro templates, rendered server-side so crawlers see it on the first response:

* **PDP:** Product + Merchant Listing Schema (`ProductGroup` + variant `Product`s), with real-time inventory driving availability.
* **PLP:** CollectionPage + BreadcrumbList + ItemList Schema (ItemList reflects the initial SSR'd product batch).
* **Boutique pages:** LocalBusiness / ClothingStore Schema per location.
* **Homepages:** Organisation + WebSite Schema per regional storefront, with per-prefix `WebSite` nodes (including the Global-e international paths `/en-ca/` and `/en-ch/`).

### 8.5 URL strategy

* Product URL: `/[prefix]/[name]-[colour].html` — the `.html` suffix is preserved to maintain existing indexed URLs.
* Category URL: `/[prefix]/[slug]` (no suffix), with 301 redirects from legacy paths.
* 301 redirects for every URL that changes as a result of migration (products, categories, content). Implemented at the CDN/edge layer to keep application-layer impact minimal.

### 8.6 GEO (DMU-042)

No GEO-specific features in launch scope. The technical foundations enabling post-launch GEO — SSR, structured data, canonicals, XML sitemaps — are in place at go-live so no architecture decision blocks future activation.

---

9. Performance Strategy
-----------------------

LCP at p75 mobile is the binding constraint and the de-facto cap on third-party script weight.

| Metric | Target |
| --- | --- |
| LCP (mobile p75) | ≤ 2 s |
| Lighthouse Performance | ≥ 0.80 |
| Lighthouse Accessibility | ≥ 0.90 |
| Lighthouse Best Practices | ≥ 0.90 |

### 9.1 Third-party defer rule

Anything loaded via Didomi callback (GTM — which loads Meta, GA4, and other GTM-housed tags via Tell No Lies; Narvar EDD widget; Inside Chat) is deferred, async-loaded, or injected post-hydration so it does not block LCP. **Measmerize** (Find My Size / size guide — PDP only) likewise defers behind LCP — the script injects after the product hero image has loaded. **reCAPTCHA** likewise loads only on register/login form interaction, so it never sits on the critical path of any other page (consent treatment per §11.1). **Exception (AAB-004):** Optimizely Web is a PWA-direct head tag (not a GTM tag) and deliberately loads in the page head **before render** to prevent A/B flicker, scoped to the US storefront where Optimizely runs. **Crazy Egg (AAB-005)** loads async and post-Didomi-consent. Both load strictly post-Didomi-consent; keep both snippets minimal.

### 9.2 Other levers

* **Images:** all storefront imagery — product and editorial — is stored in and served from **Contentful** (`images.ctfassets.net`) via the Contentful Images API; SFCC holds no image assets (DMU-010 migration de-scoped; product images CRM-075; all media via the CMS library HPC-003). The PWA generates `srcset` / `sizes` and sets size, quality, and format per breakpoint on the asset URL — **AVIF primary with WebP / JPEG fallbacks**. Lazy-load all non-LCP images; priority-load the primary hero image (PRD-064). Never render full-resolution images at thumbnail size.
* **Video:** sourced by platform, not self-hosted, so codec / adaptive-streaming selection belongs to the upstream player rather than to this layer:

  + **Product videos → Vimeo**, referenced by embed URL stored in product data or the CMS (PRD-067). Load behind a lightweight facade (poster image + click/scroll-to-load) so the Vimeo player JS never lands on the LCP critical path.
  + **Content-managed page videos → Contentful** by default, served from the Contentful asset CDN and referenced within the CMS content entry alongside the page content. Editorial pages may also embed a Vimeo video by URL where preferred (HPC-004) — the product/editorial split above is the expected pattern, not a hard restriction.
  + Across both: `preload="metadata"` by default; autoplay reserved for muted, short-loop hero clips only.
* Dynamic imports for heavy non-initial components.
* Parallel data fetches; no client-side waterfalls. Fetch only required fields.

### 9.3 Where performance is measured

The CI Lighthouse gate (§14.3) catches regressions but runs against the Dev-tier MRT deployment — slower than production hardware, further from the edge, and not representative of the LCP a real shopper experiences. The signed-off LCP and Lighthouse targets in this section are therefore validated against **Stage**, which mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier). Treat CI numbers as regression indicators; treat Stage numbers as the contractual ones.

> **SSR connection pool tuning:** the initial per-pool connection caps defined in §12.1 are derived from expected concurrency, not observed traffic. The first Stage performance run should include per-pool queue-depth and connection-wait metrics (undici emits these as diagnostic channel events). Use those numbers to validate or revise the caps.

---

10. Accessibility
-----------------

**Target:** WCAG 2.2 AA, with WCAG 2.1 AA as the floor that is always met.

**Automated coverage:**

* axe-core via `vitest-axe` at the unit layer and `axe-playwright` at the E2E layer
* Storybook a11y addon at component level during development
* Lighthouse CI accessibility score ≥ 0.90 in the SIT gate

**Manual coverage:** delegated to Zimmermann's existing accessibility vendor (unconfirmed — vendor, screen-reader / browser matrix, and audit cadence to be supplied by Zimmermann).

---

11. Consent & Marketing
-----------------------

### 11.1 Didomi gating (REG-048–056)

* Cookie consent banner on first visit, all storefronts; preferences persist across sessions and are reviewable/updatable per category at any time.
* **No third-party tracking or marketing script loads until consent is granted** — including GTM (and the tags Tell No Lies loads downstream: Meta, Pinterest, TikTok, GA4, etc.), the PWA-direct head tags Optimizely Web and Crazy Egg (AAB-004/005), Inside Chat, Narvar widgets.
* **reCAPTCHA is not a tracking script** (CRM-008). It loads on register / login form interaction only, deferred to keep it off LCP. **Regional split:** in **EU & UK** it is consent-gated and loads only after Didomi consent — with the accepted consequence that a visitor who declines consent is never challenged, so reCAPTCHA provides no bot protection there. In **all other regions** it loads on form interaction regardless of consent state.
* GTM integrated with Didomi for **Google Consent Mode v2**; hashed email passed at order confirmation for Enhanced Conversions.
* Where consent state cannot be determined, the system **fails closed** — no third-party scripts load.
* Per-storefront consent defaults are specified under REG-054.

### 11.2 Marketing opt-in sync

`FE → SFCC → Omneo → Emarsys` is the opt-in sync chain (REG-058, REG-059). Sync failures queue and retry silently — they never block the user flow. Trigger points (guest at order placement, registered at registration and My Account preference updates) are functional detail, out of scope for this TSD.

### 11.3 GDPR touchpoints in the PWA

GDPR fulfilment (DSAR, right-to-erasure, retention, breach reporting per REG-060–067) is handled by the SFCC GDPR cartridge and BM configuration — out of scope for this TSD. PWA-side touchpoints are limited to:

* Localised privacy policy pages, served from Contentful per storefront.
* The consent UI itself (covered in 11.1).
* Surfacing the customer-initiated erasure / data-export entry point in My Account where exposed by SFCC.

12. Graceful Degradation
------------------------

Each external system fails independently — one outage does not break a page.

| System | Failure mode |
| --- | --- |
| Contentful | Render page without editorial content; never block commerce data on CMS |
| Global-e | Surface explicit error; do not silently fall back to SFCC for international checkout |
| Didomi | Fail closed — no consent, no third-party scripts |
| Omneo (writes) / Emarsys | Queue and retry silently; never block the user flow |
| Omneo (reads) | **Load-bearing for My Account profile pages** — per DMU-004 only email + Omneo ID are migrated; all other customer profile data is sourced live from Omneo at login. Surface an explicit retry/error UI on profile pages if the round-trip fails; do not render stale or partial profile data. |
| Google Maps | Degrade to manual address entry; never hard-block checkout |
| AP21 (Retail Rewards) | On AP21 unavailability at the point of Rewards application, inform the customer and allow an alternative payment method |
| Narvar (EDD) | Suppress widget; do not show an error or block checkout |

### 12.1 Blast-Radius Containment

The failure modes above describe what the PWA does when a single integration is unavailable. This section covers how to limit the *spread* of an attack or outage — ensuring a degraded integration cannot consume shared resources and take down unrelated features.

#### Edge (outside the PWA — Infrastructure / SI Partner)

* **Web Application Firewalls + rate limiting** is the primary lever for volumetric attacks and credential-stuffing.
* **SFCC Business Manager** provides API-level rate limiting for SFCC endpoints, independent of the storefront edge.

#### SSR layer (inside the PWA)

`overrides/app/ssr.js` makes server-side `fetch` calls directly (token exchange, JWKS, SF Payments metadata). Node's native `fetch` is backed by `undici` internally. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS).

> **Implementation note:** the per-call `dispatcher` option is safer than the `setGlobalDispatcher` in a managed environment (MRT) since it does not touch the global dispatcher that Salesforce internal libraries may rely on. The `commerce-sdk-react` hooks manage their own HTTP client server-side (Commerce SDK) and are not affected in either approach.

The connection pool split is an engineering decision — the right pool boundaries and sizes depend on observed traffic patterns and the integration map in §7. Planned pools (connection caps should be validated later — see §9.3):

| Pool | Origin | Calls | Cap | `connectTimeout` | `bodyTimeout` | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sfcc-scapi` | `<https://{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`> | SLAS JWKS (token validation for passwordless login, reset password) | 5 | 5 s | 8 s | `jose` caches the JWK set for its rotation period; actual network calls are rare. Isolated so a JWKS fetch is never starved by higher-volume pools. |
| `sfcc-payments` | `config.app.sfPayments.metadataUrl` host (a `*.demandware.net` or SCAPI hostname — waiting confirmation from Mani) | Payment method metadata on every checkout page SSR | 10 | 5 s | 8 s | Called on every checkout page load; moderate frequency. Separate from `sfcc-scapi` because a checkout traffic spike must not consume SLAS connections. |
| `mulesoft` | `MULESOFT_BASE_URL` | Order history, order details, boutique / BOPIS stock check, GiveX balance check | 20 | 5 s | 10 s | Highest user-facing concurrency (My Account + PDP). GiveX balance calls carry payment credentials in the POST body — a slow MuleSoft response must not hold connections open and starve other pools. Highest cap reflects the broadest call surface. |
| `marketing-cloud-auth` | `<https://{subdomain}.auth.marketingcloudapis.com`> | Marketing Cloud client-credentials token exchange | 5 | 5 s | 15 s | User-triggered, infrequent; token cached at module scope for 15 min. Isolated so an MC outage cannot consume SFCC or MuleSoft connections. |
| `marketing-cloud-rest` | `<https://{subdomain}.rest.marketingcloudapis.com`> | Magic-link email send (passwordless login, reset password) | 5 | 5 s | 15 s | Same trigger as above; higher body timeout because email delivery APIs can respond slowly under load. |
| `google-places` | `<https://places.googleapis.com`> (Places API — New) | Address autocomplete at checkout (CFD-023, CFD-030, CFD-059) | 5 | 3 s | 5 s | Non-critical-path; graceful fallback to manual entry. Short timeouts ensure a Places API slowdown releases connections quickly. |
| `booxi` | Booxi base URL (TBD) | Boutique appointment read in My Account (CRM-165–167) | 5 | 3 s | 5 s | My Account only; non-critical-path within that page. |

**Contentful:** The Contentful SDK (`contentful` v11) does not expose a `dispatcher` hook on its internal fetch calls, so connection isolation for Contentful is not achievable through this pattern. Primary mitigation is the graceful degradation rule in §12 (Render page without editorial content).

---

13. Testing Strategy
--------------------

Three layers, no duplicated coverage — the cheapest layer that proves a behaviour wins.

| Layer | Tool | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | Vitest | Pure logic, data mapping, transforms, isolated hooks |
| Component interaction | Storybook `play` | Single-component user interactions |
| E2E | Playwright | Full journeys, multi-region, integration boundaries |

### 13.1 What is tested

Failure paths that would be non-obvious or costly to debug: Contentful → component data mapping, locale / currency transforms, Global-e pricing / tax branching, checkout ownership, consent gating, cart mutations, optimistic-update rollback. Framework behaviour and pure visual rendering are not tested at this layer.

### 13.2 E2E gherkin-first workflow

Every Playwright spec starts as a Gherkin `.feature` file that Lead QA validates in plain English before any code is written. This prevents technically correct tests of the wrong behaviour.

### 13.3 Multi-region fixtures

E2E specs are parameterised by `SITE_ID` from day one — every journey runs across all 8 storefronts and 11 active locales, with site-specific `baseUrl`, currency, checkout owner, tax model, and consent default supplied by a fixture rather than hardcoded. (Because a test hardcoded to one region cannot be cheaply expanded later)

### 13.4 Selector priority

Tests select elements the way users and assistive tech perceive them: accessible selectors (role + name, label, visible text) first, semantic HTML attributes second (`alt`, `title`), `data-testid` only when nothing semantic applies. Tag/class/DOM-position selectors are not used. This doubles as a continuous accessibility check.

---

14. CI/CD & Environments
------------------------

This section probably belong to a DevOps TSD, but will put here temporarily until we have one.

### 14.1 Topology

A six-tier environment topology spans **Local → Dev → SIT → Stage → UAT → Prod**. Each tier (other than Local) has its own SFCC realm, Contentful environment, and MuleSoft connections. Ownership splits across three zones — Digital, IT/NewStore, and Shared (Digital + Business).

| # | Tier | Owner | Purpose | Third-party availability | Deploy trigger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Local** | Digital | Feature build on developer machines | All services mocked (MSW stubs) | `npm start` |
| 2 | **Dev** | Digital | Integrated digital testing across all 6 storefronts, independent of NewStore | MuleSoft STG · NewStore Dev · Omneo STG · Narvar stub · Adyen sandbox | Merge to `develop` |
| 3 | **SIT** | IT / NewStore | NewStore SIT and regression on its own cadence | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Narvar STG · AP21 test | NewStore release cadence (parallel lane, non-blocking for Digital releases) |
| 4 | **Stage** (E2E) | Shared | End-to-end testing with all third parties live; time-boxed booked windows | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Omneo STG · Narvar STG · Adyen sandbox | Booked 2-week window |
| 5 | **UAT** | Shared | Business acceptance across all 6 regions | NewStore STG · Narvar STG · Omneo STG · Adyen sandbox | Business approval gate |
| 6 | **Prod** | Live | Production; AU canary then flag-flip to remaining regions | NewStore PROD · MuleSoft PROD · Omneo PROD · Narvar PROD · Adyen PROD | Release manager + canary gate |

Stage is the **contractual performance-test environment** referenced in §9.3 — it mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle class, CDN/edge configuration, SFCC realm tier).

### 14.2 Branch model

GitFlow with explicit back-merges to keep `develop` aligned with production.

| Branch | Branched from | Merges to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `feature/*` | `develop` | `develop` |
| `fix/*` | `develop` | `develop` |
| `release/*` | `develop` | `main` **and** `develop` |
| `fix/release-{version}-*` | the `release/*` branch | the `release/*` branch (forward-merged to `develop` via the release back-merge) |
| `hotfix/*` | `main` | `main` **and** `develop` |
| `develop`, `main` | — | protected; PR-only |

Release branches are supervised — code logic fixes go on a `fix/release-{version}-*` sub-branch rather than directly on the release branch. Releases and hotfixes always back-merge to `develop` so production fixes flow forward automatically.

### 14.3 CI workflows

**QA workflow (**`qa.yml`) — runs on every PR to `develop` and `release/**`. Code-correctness checks with no environment dependency:

* Unit tests (Vitest)
* Storybook interaction tests (`play` functions) and component-level accessibility checks via `@storybook/addon-a11y` (`storybook test --ci`)

**SIT gate (**`digital-sit.yml`) — runs on push/PR to `release/**`; on merge to `develop` it also deploys to the **Dev** environment (tier 2 in §14.1). Environment-dependent checks:

* Playwright `p0` priority specs
* Bundle-size check against the ceilings in §9
* Contract tests against the MuleSoft OpenAPI specification
* Lighthouse CI thresholds (Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90)
* Trend gate against the LHCI history server

### 14.4 Deployment

Deployment is via Salesforce Managed Runtime. Each tier maps to its own MRT target:

* **Dev** — deployed on merge to `develop`, gated on a clean SIT gate (§14.3)
* **SIT** — deployed on the NewStore release cadence, isolated from the Digital release path (failures do not block `release/**`)
* **Stage** — deployed on a booked 2-week window for full end-to-end testing with live third parties
* **UAT** — deployed for business acceptance; promotion requires Business sign-off
* **Prod** — release-manager-gated; AU canary first, then flag-flip to remaining regions

Production deploys are gated on a clean SIT gate run plus stakeholder approval through Stage and UAT.

MRT deployment targets map one-to-one to the topology: `dev | sit | stage | uat | production`.",

Confluence, and JIRA (an Explore agent independently re-checked all 11 angles: file content,
repo-wide grep, every fetch call, git log, package.json deps, existing test coverage, doc text,

added: the 7 pools split into two groups — 4 (`sfcc-scapi`, `sfcc-payments`, `marketing-cloud-auth`,
`marketing-cloud-rest`) correspond to integrations with real, currently-shipping `fetch()` calls
that bypass their pool today; the other 3 (`mulesoft`, `google-places`, `booxi`) correspond to
features with **no implementation at all yet** — those pools were built speculatively, ahead of
the feature code. Both groups are "100% unused," just for different reasons. Also confirmed:
`overrides/app/ssr/` (where all 4 relevant files live) is Tier 1 in three separate rule docs
(`frozenFiles.md`, `.cursor/rules/tier1FrozenFiles.mdc`, `copilot-instructions.md`) — a plausible
institutional reason the gap has persisted, not just oversight.

ticket's job to fix, but good to know it's already flagged elsewhere.

352419841 template in practice** — worth matching its conventions: lists multiple authors/
reviewers when more than one person contributed (here: Gideon should likely appear alongside
Tim, matching how SFCC-249 lists both a BA Lead and a Solution Architect as reviewers, since the
ticket names both Gideon and Angelo as required collaborators); adds a `References` section at
the end (not in the raw template but clearly accepted practice); uses Appendices for

authority) is on record expecting SFCC-237's TSD as a separate deliverable: *"MRT-app architecture
is out of scope here; covered by a separate TSD (SFCC-237). — Keep this TSD scoped to one
problem."* — direct corroboration that Tim is tracking this and expects it to land.

underlying files (git log confirms zero commits to the flagged files since 07-30).

recommendation (§3-4) genuinely cannot be finalised without the Gideon/platform conversation
above — surface that to the user before drafting those sections rather than guessing at platform
capability or cost. **Track this work against SFCC-681 going forward, not SFCC-237.**

Verified 2026-08-05 against the real `.github/workflows/` + `gh` API. Several docs disagree with each other and with the code. Flag these (doc-integrity rule) before wiring release/promotion tooling; do not silently pick one.

1. **Test tier existence — CORRECTED 2026-08-10: `.docs/architecture.md` is also stale, not an exception.** Confluence "Environment Topology & Promotion Path" (page 304840708, still v4 as of 2026-08-10) describes a 6-tier model **with no Test tier** (LOCAL→DEV→SIT→STAGE→UAT→PROD). This entry originally also listed `.docs/architecture.md` as correctly including Test — **that was wrong**; a fresh full read of `.docs/architecture.md`'s own "Environments" table (2026-08-10) shows the identical 6-row Local/Dev/SIT/UAT/Stage/Prod table with **no Test row**, and `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md §14.1` carries the exact same 6-row table verbatim (same staleness, shared/copied content). So `.docs/architecture.md` and `tsd-architecture.md` are stale on this point **the same way** the Confluence topology page is — not a source that contradicts it. What *does* correctly include Test: 05.6 Environment Details (285540356), the tag proposal (335216656), SFCC-254, `.claude/rules/tagging.md` (repo governance file, correct), and the actual `deploy-test.yml` + `test` GitHub Environment + `deploy-then-gate` bundle-size job (live).

2. **Promotion order (Stage vs UAT).** Topology page 304840708 orders **STAGE → UAT** (Stage = convergence, then UAT business acceptance). `.docs/architecture.md` and the tag proposal order **UAT → STAGE → PROD**. Genuinely different sequencing — needs a team decision; affects promotion tooling.

3. **SIT trigger model.** Topology page + 05.6 say SIT **auto-deploys on every `develop` push** after sit-gate. Reality: `deploy-sit.yml` triggers on `workflow_run` of **"SIT Gate" (digital-sit.yml) completing on `release/**`** — SIT is release-branch-driven, not develop-driven. `.docs/memory/projectState.md` has this right; the Confluence pages don't. (This is the tag proposal's still-open Question 3.)

4. **GitHub Environment names.** Topology page's secret-scope table names `pre-prod` and `production`; the **actual** environments are `staging` and `prod`. `deploy-stg.yml` binds `environment: staging` (filename says `stg`); `deploy-prod.yml` binds `prod` but the MRT push target is `production`. Version-guard/promotion tooling must key off the real names (`dev/test/sit/uat/staging/prod`) — the `stg`≠`staging` mismatch already caused a bug once (commit 12bf91b).

5. **CI/CD architecture stale.** "PWA CI/CD Pipeline" (305561601) and "7.1c Checklist" (305430530) describe `deploy-sit` as a **job inside `digital-sit.yml`** and list the `sit` environment + MRT secrets as not-yet-created. Reality: separate `deploy-*.yml` workflows, and all six environments exist. 7.1c/305561601 need a refresh.

6. **`mobify.config.js` referenced but absent.** frozenFiles.md (Tier 1), `protected-file-guard.yml`/`qa.yml` path filters, `architecture.md`, and 7.1c all reference `mobify.config.js` — the file **does not exist**. `package.json` has no `mobify` key (uses `ccExtensibility`). MRT config actually lives in `config/default.js` `ssrParameters`. Verify where the MRT project slug for `pwa-kit-dev push` actually resolves from.

7. **Bundle-size budget mismatch (found 2026-08-06 during Step 7 V&V).** Topology 304840708's DEV-gate lists `vendor.js < 250 kB` + a `main.css < 50 kB` check. Reality: `package.json` `bundlesize` = `main.js ≤ 180 kB`, `vendor.js ≤ 550 kB`, **no main.css check**. Material: the actual vendor.js build is ~515 kB — passes the real 550 budget, would FAIL the doc's 250. Doc budget is less than half the real one.

8. **architecture.md (repo doc) also carries the stale naming (found 2026-08-06).** `.docs/architecture.md:108` says MRT targets in `mobify.config.js` map `dev|sit|uat|stage|production` — uses `stage`/`production` (topology naming), not the real `staging`/`prod` env names, AND references the absent `mobify.config.js` (conflict #6). So D's reconciliation is NOT Confluence-only — a repo doc is stale too.
9. **Confluence ALSO repeats the `mobify.config.js` myth (found 2026-08-10, during SFCC-237 research).** 05.6 Environment Details (285540356)'s "SIT — Operational Details → Config" section: "MRT push credentials (`MRT_USER`, `MRT_API_KEY`)... scoped to the project slug in `mobify.config.js`." Root-caused during SFCC-237 work: `@salesforce/pwa-kit-dev@3.18.0`'s `getConfig()` (via `cosmiconfig`) never searches for a root `mobify.config.js` at all in this version — it resolves `config/{target}.js` → `config/local.js` → `config/default.js` → `package.json`'s `mobify` key, and the project slug actually comes from `package.json`'s `"name"` field. So conflict #6 isn't repo-docs-only either — it's now confirmed on Confluence too. Full detail in [[project_sfcc237_mrt_topology_spike]].
10. **335216656 (tag proposal) still v18 as of 2026-08-10 — Q3's decision not yet written back.** The `[[project_tagbased_rollout_decisions]]` Q3 decision (SIT stays branch/gate-driven, Option B, decided 2026-08-05) has not been recorded on the Confluence page itself — Open Question 3 there still reads as unresolved. Not a new conflict, just confirming the "still needs Tim" gap from that memory hasn't closed yet.

**How to apply:** When advising on release/deploy topology, trust the code + `gh` live state over the Confluence topology pages AND over `.docs/architecture.md`/`tsd-architecture.md` (both share the same stale Test-tier gap — see corrected point #1). `.claude/rules/tagging.md` is the one repo doc confirmed accurate on tiers. Treat 304840708/305561601/7.1c/285540356/architecture.md as all needing updates on one point or another. See [[project-release-branch-status]] and [[project_sfcc237_mrt_topology_spike]].

This is a concrete, specific finding for the test: `sendMagicLinkEmail` has zero error handling around its Marketing Cloud calls, creating a genuine unhandled-rejection risk in the codebase. The other handlers like `jwksCaching` and `paymentMetadataHandler` properly catch failures and convert them to HTTP error responses, but this one doesn't.
